In this course, you're learning how to use evals to find out whether
the applications you build are doing the job you want them to do.

And as you've seen, that can be challenging,
because mistakes in AI applications can be subtle.

For example, the application might keep running without an error
message or a failing test and still do something wrong.

So you need to look carefully at what your application actually does
and compare that with what you expected.
If those don't match, you've found a problem to investigate and fix.

In module one, you focused on seeing what the
application actually did.

You learned to make requests, run the application,
and use traces to follow the steps it took.

But seeing what the application did is only one
part of the comparison.

So in this video, you'll learn how to find and develop requirements
that describe what your application must do and must not do.

Those requirements tell you what to test for and what
would count as a failure.

At the end of this module, those requirements will become part of a
benchmark, a reusable set of cases, expected outcomes,
and labels you can run as the application changes.

You'll do this in three steps. First, you'll find requirements
and write them down.

then you'll turn specific observations into requirements
that cover more than one case.

Finally, you'll review what you've written for unclear wording
or situations you haven't covered.

So let's start by exploring some sources for requirements.
There are three useful places to look.

As you explore each one, ask yourself, "What does this tell me the
application should do or should avoid doing?"
Your goal is to write down that expectation as a requirement.
To see how this works,

let's look at an application that helps an animal shelter arrange
outings where volunteers take dogs out for the day.

It checks whether volunteers are eligible, matches them with suitable
dogs, and helps schedule the outings.
Now, the first place to look is existing rules.

For example, an animal shelter may have a rule that volunteers with a
do-not-adopt flag cannot take dogs on outings.

Ask yourself, what does the application need to do
to follow that rule?

If it arranges these outings, it must not match a flagged volunteer
with any dog. That's a requirement.

Notice that you don't need to see the application make that mistake
before adding this requirement.

The shelter's rule already tells you what should happen,
but not every expectation has been written down,
so the second place to look is people who understand the work.

They may know what the application should do in situations the
existing rules don't address.

For the shelter application, you could talk to staff who regularly
match volunteers with dogs.

Ask what they consider when making a match and what would
make them reject one.

As they explain, ask yourself, what should the application do to
make the same decision?

Now, people close to the work may not think of every requirement
just because you asked.

It can be easier to explain why they would accept or reject a
particular match than to list every rule they use.

So you can show them a set of volunteer descriptions and dog records,
and ask which matches they would recommend and why.

Use their explanations to write down what the
application should do and when.

keep the reason with the requirement, so it's clear why the
application should behave that way.

Talking to others helps you understand what should happen, but it's
hard to anticipate every requirement through discussion alone.
So the third place to look is the application's traces.

Looking directly at how the application handles requests can reveal
situations you hadn't considered.

One place to start is with traces you've already saved,
whether they came from real users or requests you tried yourself.

If you don't have traces yet, write a few realistic requests yourself
or with an LLM and run them through the application.
This lets you start learning from behavior before you have real users.

Now, let's use the Northwind application from your labs to see how a
trace can help you write a requirement.
A customer asks, "How should I care for my merino wool sweater?"

The application answers, "You can machine wash it on a wool cycle
and then tumble dry."

To check that advice, you look at the product information the
application received, which is recorded in the trace.
It says machine washable on wool cycle. It says nothing about drying.

So the washing advice comes from the product information, but the
application added drying advice it didn't have the information for,
and that could ruin the sweater.

You could record the mistake like this:
the application recommended tumble drying,
even though it had no drying instructions for this sweater.

Keep that note with the trace and the product information, so you have
a record of what went wrong and why you judged it a mistake.

To turn that observation into a requirement, ask yourself,
what should the application do to avoid this kind of mistake?

You could tell it not to recommend tumble-drying this sweater,
but it could still invent other instructions for another product.
You need a requirement that covers those recommendations too.

So you could write, "Only make claims about products that are
supported by Northwind data."
That requirement is broader than the sweater case.

It can also catch unsupported claims about sizing, color,
availability, care instructions, or return policies.

Now, when you review what the application says about a
product, you can ask,

"Does the Northwind data support what the
application told the customer?"
That helps you catch invented details about other products too.

Keep any further examples with their traces and notes,
so you can use them to test and refine the requirement.

So that was the first step where you find and
develop your requirements.
The second step is to review and refine what you've written.
Look for unclear wording and situations you haven't covered,

so you can improve the requirements and see what still
needs to be worked out.

There are two useful things to check.
First, look for words in your requirements that need more explanation.

For example, "Recommend a suitable dog" depends on what
you mean by "suitable".

If you leave that unexplained, whoever evaluates the recommendation
has to supply their own interpretation.

To make "suitable" more specific, you could start by asking what would
make a match unsuitable. The shelter's rules can help you answer that.

For example, a dog that requires an experienced handler should not be
matched with a volunteer who lacks that experience.

Write that restriction into the requirement. You're taking a rule
that was hidden inside the word "suitable" and making it explicit.

Now, a person or an LLM evaluating the recommendation can check
that rule instead of guessing what you meant.
Second, look for situations your requirements don't yet cover.

It's easy to describe what should happen when the application has
complete information,

but it's harder to spot what it should do when that information is
missing or conflicting.

For the shelter, also check what the application should do
when none of the suitable dogs are available.

Check whether the shelter has a rule for that situation.
If it does, add what the application should do to your requirements.

If it doesn't, you need to decide what should happen when no
suitable dog is available.

Until that's settled, you won't know whether the application handled
the situation correctly.

You've learned how to find requirements and review them for unclear
wording and situations you may have missed.
This helps you spell out what your application should do.

But to find out whether your application meets those requirements,
you need requests that put each one to the test.
So in the next video,

you'll learn to build test sets that cover different situations
for your requirements
and spell out what the application should do in each.
I'll see you there.
